title: Google Expands Gemini & Search: New Dev Platform Adds More Connected Apps, Boosting Integration
body:
Google unveiled a new Connected Apps Platform that will let a broader range of third‑party developers embed their services directly into Gemini, the company’s AI‑driven chatbot, and into Google Search. The move is positioned as a “unified” framework that expands the ecosystem of apps that can surface contextual answers, automate tasks, and provide real‑time data without leaving the Google interface. By opening the platform to more developers, Google hopes to turn Gemini and Search into a hub for actionable, on‑demand services, ranging from travel bookings to productivity tools, while tightening the integration of its AI capabilities with everyday web experiences.

The announcement builds on an existing set of Connected Apps that currently include services such as Kayak, Instacart, and Duolingo, which already allow users to retrieve flight details, order groceries, or practice a new language directly from a chat prompt. Under the new platform, developers will gain access to a standardized API, authentication flow, and UI guidelines that streamline the process of exposing app functionality to Gemini’s conversational interface and to Search’s rich result cards. Google says the framework will support “real‑time data, secure authentication, and deep linking,” enabling actions like completing a purchase, checking a bank balance, or updating a calendar event without opening a separate app or website.

Industry analysts see the expansion as part of Google’s broader strategy to make its AI products more indispensable than traditional search. By embedding third‑party capabilities, Google can keep users within its own ecosystem longer, potentially capturing more ad revenue and data signals. The move also mirrors moves by rivals such as Microsoft, which has been integrating OpenAI’s models into its Office suite and Bing search, and Apple, which is deepening Siri’s third‑party app support. However, Google’s advantage lies in its massive user base and the seamless search experience that can surface these apps alongside organic results, giving developers a high‑visibility channel that many competitors lack.

From a developer perspective, the platform promises a lower barrier to entry. Previously, integrating with Gemini required bespoke code and limited documentation, restricting participation to larger tech firms. The new unified SDK includes pre‑built UI components, sandbox testing environments, and detailed analytics dashboards, allowing startups and niche service providers to prototype and launch Connected Apps more quickly. Google also emphasized security, stating that all third‑party interactions will be subject to rigorous OAuth verification and data‑privacy audits, a response to growing concerns about AI‑mediated data sharing.

The rollout will begin with a closed beta later this quarter, inviting select partners to test the integration workflow and provide feedback on performance and user experience. Google plans to open the platform to the wider developer community by early next year, with a public documentation portal and a marketplace where users can discover and enable new Connected Apps within Gemini and Search settings. Early adopters will be able to showcase their apps in “Action Cards” that appear directly in search results or as interactive snippets in chat, offering a glimpse of a more transactional search experience.

Looking ahead, the Connected Apps Platform could reshape how users interact with the web, turning search from a passive information retrieval tool into an active gateway for completing tasks. If adoption grows as Google anticipates, the line between search, AI assistance, and app functionality may blur, prompting competitors to accelerate their own integration efforts. For developers, the platform offers a compelling new avenue to reach billions of users, while for Google, it represents a strategic step toward cementing Gemini and Search as the central command centers of everyday digital life.
